conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a quick tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days—nothing you need to prepare for. Your answers are completely confidential, and the goal is to make sure we catch anything early so we can get you the right support. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions together, one by one.

To start:  
Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I guess… I can still laugh sometimes, but mostly it feels like a lot of effort. My sister sent me a silly video yesterday and I managed a chuckle, yet it faded fast—nothing really feels light or funny the way it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly yes, but not the way I used to. I can still crack a smile if something’s genuinely funny, yet it feels forced or fades quickly—like the joy doesn’t last.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. Even little things I used to like—watching a show, meeting a friend for coffee—feel like chores now. Sometimes I make myself do them hoping I’ll feel better, but the excitement just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I’m failing him somehow. Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still replay every little thing and wonder what I should’ve done better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, everything fine on paper, and suddenly my chest feels tight—like something awful is about to happen. Most of the time I can’t even name what I’m scared of; it’s just this constant hum of worry that I can’t switch off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week I’ll be rocking the baby in the chair and out of nowhere my heart starts racing, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something terrible is about to happen. It passes after a couple of minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge for the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

They have, yeah. Most days I feel like I’m drowning in little things—dishes piling up, the baby won’t settle, texts I haven’t answered—and I just freeze. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but it feels like too much all at once.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with everything I did wrong that day or might mess up tomorrow. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake for no reason and can’t get back to sleep. It’s like the sadness just sits on my chest once the house is quiet.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be feeding the baby or folding laundry and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason. The sadness isn’t always sharp, but it’s constant—like I’m stuck in it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… probably three or four times this week. Sometimes it’s because the baby won’t stop fussing and I feel useless, other times it just hits me out of nowhere and the tears come. I try to keep quiet so my partner doesn’t worry, but it feels like the only release I have.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless at times, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind. I just want to feel like myself again so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Summary – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report; responses indicate moderate–severe distress.

Symptoms/Concerns  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Generalized anxiety, episodic panic (HR, breathlessness)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to rumination  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, “drowning”  
- No anhedonia in mild form—pleasure markedly blunted  
- No self-harm ideation endorsed  

Pattern  
Consistent with mood and anxiety spectrum common in postpartum period; intensity suggests probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety symptoms.

Screening Significance  
- Elevated score range for postpartum depression and anxiety  
- Functional impairment: infant care, home management, social withdrawal  
- Protective factor: strong infant-safety motivation; denies self-harm  

Safety  
No suicidal or infanticidal ideation reported; no plan or intent.

Next Step  
Recommend formal diagnostic interview and discussion of evidence-based treatment options (psychotherapy ± medication).
